'''''Symphoricarpos albus''''' is a species of flowering plant in the [[Caprifoliaceae|honeysuckle family]] known by the common name '''common snowberry'''.<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SYAL|taxon=Symphoricarpos albus|accessdate=4 December 2015}}</ref> Native to [[North America]], it is browsed by some animals and planted for [[ornamental plant|ornamental]] and ecological purposes, but is poisonous to humans.

== Description ==
''S. albus'' is an erect, [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] that produces a stiff, branching main stem and often several smaller shoots from a [[rhizome]]. It can spread and colonise an area to form a dense thicket.<ref name="fs">{{FEIS|genus=Symphoricarpos|species=albus|type=shrub|last=McWilliams|first=Jack|date=2000}}</ref> It reaches {{convert|1|-|2|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} in maximum height. The [[leaves]] are oppositely arranged on the spreading branches. They are generally oval in shape and vary in size, growing up to {{convert|5|cm|in|abbr=off|frac=4}} long, or slightly larger on the shoots. The [[inflorescence]] is a [[raceme]] of up to 16 flowers. Each flower has a small, five-toothed calyx of [[sepal]]s. The bell-shaped, rounded corolla is approximately {{convert|0.5|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=8}} long and is bright pink in colour. It has pointed lobes at the mouth, and the inside is filled with white hairs. The fruit is a fleshy white [[Berry (botany)|berry]]-like [[drupe]] measuring around 1 cm in diameter, containing two seeds. The plant mainly reproduces [[vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]] by sprouting from its spreading rhizome, but sometimes via seed.<ref name="fs" /> Birds [[biological dispersal|disperse]] the seeds after they eat the fruit.<ref name="fs" />

==Varieties==

There are two [[Variety (botany)|varieties]]:
*'''''S. albus'' var. ''albus''''', native to eastern North America
*'''''S. albus'' var. ''laevigatus''''', native to the Pacific coast. It is a larger shrub, up to {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} tall, with slightly larger fruit. Some [[botanist]]s treat it as a distinct species, '''''Symphoricarpos rivularis'''''.
{{clear left}}

== Distribution and habitat ==
''S. albus'' occurs across much of [[Canada]] and the northern and western United States.<ref>{{BONAP|genus=Symphoricarpos|species=albus|date=2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Jones |first=George Neville |date=1940 |title=A monograph of the genus ''Symphoricarpos'' |url=https://biodiversitylibrary.org/page/8370317<!-- page 214 --> |journal=Journal of the Arnold Arboretum |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=214-218<!-- treatment of Symphoricarpus albus -->}}</ref>

It grows in shady and moist mountain and forest habitat, in woodlands and on [[floodplain]]s and riverbanks. It can grow in a wide variety of habitat types.<ref name="fs" /> It is [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in parts of Britain, where it has been planted as an [[ornamental plant|ornamental]] and cover for game animals.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Gilbert |first=O. L. |date=1995 |title=''Symphoricarpos albus'' (L.) S. F. Blake (''S. rivularis'' Suksd., ''S. racemosus'' Michaux) |journal=Journal of Ecology |volume=83 |issue=1 |pages=159–66 |doi=10.2307/2261160 |jstor=2261160}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
This shrub is an important food source for a number of animals, including [[bighorn sheep]], [[white-tailed deer]], and [[grizzly bear]]s.<ref name="fs" /> Livestock such as [[cattle]] and [[sheep]] readily browse it.<ref name="fs" /> Many birds and small mammals use it for food and cover.<ref name="fs" /> [[Pocket gopher]]s dig burrows underneath it during the winter.<ref name="fs" />

== Toxicity ==
The fruit and shrub are poisonous to humans, causing vomiting.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lewis |first=Walter H. |date=1979-12-14 |title=Snowberry (Symphoricarpos) Poisoning in Children |journal=JAMA: The Journal of the American Medical Association |language=en |volume=242 |issue=24 |pages=2663 |doi=10.1001/jama.1979.03300240009006 |issn=0098-7484 |pmid=501855}}</ref>

== Uses ==
[[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] used the plant as medicine, [[soap]], and the wood was good for [[arrow]] shafts.<ref name=fs/> In Russia, the berries are crushed in the hands and rubbed about for a soothing folk-remedy hand lotion.{{No source|date=January 2021}}

This shrub is used for [[erosion]] control in riparian areas, and it is planted in [[ecological restoration]] projects on disturbed sites, such as abandoned mines.<ref name=fs/> Its white fruits and blue-green foliage made it a popular ornamental plant,<ref name=fs/> planted around old houses from the 1890s to the 1920s, similar to the Vanhoutte spirea or bridal wreath. It is still sold by some large, diverse conventional nurseries and native plant nurseries, and can be found occasionally in modern landscapes. It thrives in full sun or partial shade and in well-drained soil with a [[Soil pH|pH]] range of about 6.0 to 8.5. It is easy to transplant thanks to its fibrous, shallow root system. It fares well in [[U.S. Department of Agriculture]] [[hardiness zone]]s of 2 to 7.

The plant is popular among children in Germany, who play with its ripe berries due to the popping sound they make when thrown on the ground. Because of this the plant, and specifically its berries, are also called {{Lang|de|[[Bang snaps|Knallerbsen]]}} in [[German language|German]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Monning |first1=Eva |date=26 November 2021 |title=Gewöhnliche Schneebeere: Der Knallerbsenstrauch |url=https://www.mein-schoener-garten.de/pflanzen/schneebeeren/gewoehnliche-schneebeere-knallerbsenstrauch |website=Mein schöner Garten |language=de |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240711041123/https://www.mein-schoener-garten.de/pflanzen/schneebeeren/gewoehnliche-schneebeere-knallerbsenstrauch |archive-date=11 July 2024 |access-date=30 July 2025}}</ref>
